You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Step-by-step diagnosis:

1. The failing test shows that ClassUtils.getShortClassName(String[].class) returns "String;" (with a trailing semicolon), which is incorrect—expected "String[]".

2. The current bug report confirms this behavior: the semicolon is introduced at the end of the short class name for arrays.

3. Looking at ClassUtils.getShortClassName(Class<?> cls), it simply calls getShortClassName(cls.getName()) passing the class name string.

4. The code of getShortClassName(String className) method:
   - Checks for null or empty input and returns empty string accordingly.
   - Then it contains comments saying "// Handle array encoding" and "// Strip Object type encoding" but there is no actual implementation seen in the snippet for handling array class names or stripping array/object encoding.
   - It extracts the short name by taking substring after the last dot ('.') and replaces inner class separator character ('$') with package separator ('.') if any.
   - It returns this substring as the short class name.

5. For array types, the class name string returned by cls.getName() follows a JVM internal format, for example:
   - A single dimensional string array: "[Ljava.lang.String;"
   - A multidimensional array: "[[Ljava.lang.String;"
   
   The current method does not handle this format to produce a user-friendly class name. It instead uses the raw class name string, resulting in trailing semicolon and/or other JVM-specific characters being included.

6. This explains the observed bug: the trailing semicolon appears because the getShortClassName(String) method does not interpret or decode the JVM array encoded name format but treats it as a normal string.

7. No recent bug reports are directly related or helpful in this specific context.

Conclusion: The root cause is missing code logic in ClassUtils.getShortClassName(String) to detect and properly decode internal array type encoding strings like "[Ljava.lang.String;" into readable class names like "String[]". This results in trailing semicolons and other unwanted symbols appearing in the returned short class name.

Suggested fix is to add proper handling of arrays (and possibly primitives arrays) inside getShortClassName(String) method before extracting the substring after the last dot.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test failure and current bug report show that ClassUtils.getShortClassName returns a type name with an unwanted trailing semicolon for array classes, e.g. "String;". The method ClassUtils.getShortClassName(Class<?>) simply invokes getShortClassName(String) with the class's name. The getShortClassName(String) method currently lacks logic to handle JVM internal class names for arrays (e.g., "[Ljava.lang.String;"). It treats the array-encoded class name as a normal string, extracting the substring after the last '.' and returning that result. Since the internal name for a String array ends with a semicolon, this semicolon ends up in the returned short name. There is commented code hinting at handling array encoding and object type encoding, but no implementation is present. This explains the bug fully. Thus, the bug is caused by missing decoding of JVM array type signatures in getShortClassName(String) leading to trailing semicolons or other internal characters appearing in the result.

Suggested fix: Implement proper detection and decoding of array internal names in getShortClassName(String), translating "[Ljava.lang.String;" to "String[]" and similarly for other types.

Best methods to fix:
ClassUtils.getShortClassName(java.lang.String)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug.
